title: You Are Not Perceiving the World, You Are Predicting It: Your Brain Fabricates the Reality You See
dek: Perception is not the passive reception of external signals but a prediction the brain makes based on the body's internal state; the world and the self you experience are a controlled hallucination constrained by sensory input, and all of it ultimately serves to keep you alive.
why: A TED-style talk that uses three experiments — the checkerboard, noise, and the rubber hand — to explain predictive processing, and gives a clear answer to whether AI can be sentient. Good as an introduction; light on cutting-edge detail.
who: Engineers working on AI consciousness or brain-computer interfaces, founders trying to judge whether AI will have self-awareness, and tech investors who need to distinguish intelligence from feeling.
skip: Listeners already familiar with predictive processing can skip the checkerboard and noise demonstrations at 5:10-10:20 and go straight to the section on the self.

points.h: General anesthesia is not sleep, it is complete nonexistence
points.body: The speaker disappeared completely for the third time during a general anesthetic: as the drug flooded his brain he felt detached, fragmented and cold, and then he woke up, but in between there was no sense of elapsed time at all. Waking from deep sleep, you know how long you were out; waking from general anesthesia it could have been 5 minutes, 5 hours, 5 years or even 50 years — he simply was not there. This complete disappearance is worth taking seriously because it turns "how does consciousness happen" into one of the biggest remaining puzzles in science and philosophy: how do billions of neurons produce the you of right now.

points.h: You see what your brain expects to see
points.body: The brain is locked inside the skull, with no light and no sound, and all it gets is streams of electrical impulses that relate to external objects only indirectly. So perception is not a readout of the world but an informed guess: the brain combines sensory signals with prior expectations about what the world is "probably like" and guesses the most likely cause. In the checkerboard shadow illusion, squares A and B are exactly the same gray, but because the visual cortex prior knows that "shadows darken surfaces," B is seen as brighter; the same meaningless noise suddenly reveals words once you have heard the original sentence. The sensory input has not changed — only the brain's guess about its cause.

points.h: The world is generated from the inside out
points.body: Since perception is active guessing, the brain does not form experience only from sensory signals coming in from outside; equally or even more important are the predictions traveling inward. A Sussex team's demonstration processed campus video with a Deep Dream-like algorithm to simulate what the brain sees when "prediction is too strong": dogs everywhere, and the picture turns into something like a hallucinatory state or the visual experience of psychosis. The conclusion is steep: if hallucination is perception out of control, then normal perception right now is also a hallucination, just a controlled one — the brain's predictions held in check by sensory signals from the world.

points.h: The self is also a hallucination the brain generates
points.body: The experience of being "you" is likewise generated by the brain, and it is not just one thing: there is the experience of having a body and of being a body, the experience of perceiving the world from a first-person perspective, the experience of intending to act and being the cause of events in the world, and the "distinct personality that persists over time" maintained by memory and social interaction. Psychiatry and neurology already know these dimensions can be pulled apart from one another. The so-called unified and continuous self is in fact a rather fragile construction of the brain, and like vision it needs explaining.

points.h: The brain will claim a fake hand
points.body: The rubber hand illusion can be done at home: the real hand is hidden, a fake hand is placed in front of you, two brushes stroke the real and fake hands at the same time, and the subject keeps staring at the fake hand. After a while the fake hand vaguely becomes part of one's own body. The reason is that vision and touch agree, the shape looks like a hand, and the position is roughly where a hand should be — enough evidence for the brain to guess "this is my hand." Threaten the fake hand directly with a hammer and you can see that the subject has taken it into their own body. Sussex's Peter Lush found that the strength of this illusion is highly correlated with hypnotic suggestibility: the experimental setup itself suggests "the fake hand belongs to you," so people who are easily suggestible naturally find it easier to have that experience.

points.h: A heartbeat in sync makes the fake hand feel more like your own
points.body: Besides viewing the body as an external object, the brain also senses the body from the inside, which is called interoception: heartbeat, blood pressure and visceral states are constantly telling the brain how things are inside. This kind of perception is often ignored, but it is precisely what keeps the body alive. In a VR version of the rubber hand experiment in the Sussex lab, the virtual hand flashed red and black either in sync or out of sync with the heartbeat; when it was in sync with the heartbeat, subjects were clearly more likely to feel it was part of their own body. Body ownership is thus shown to be deeply rooted in the perception of the internal body.

points.h: Interoception is not knowing, it is staying alive
points.body: Experience from inside the body is completely different from seeing the external world: you do not perceive "the kidney is here, the liver is there, the spleen is somewhere," and the viscera barely enter consciousness unless something goes wrong with them. This is because the brain's purpose in interoception is not to judge what is there but to control and regulate, holding physiological variables such as blood pressure and heart rate within a narrow range suitable for survival. When prediction is used to identify external objects, we experience it as "seeing something"; when prediction is used to regulate the body, we experience it as whether control is going smoothly. So the most basic experience of the self is directly rooted in the mechanisms that keep the organism alive.

points.h: A smarter computer is not the same as a conscious one
points.body: Finally, three consequences. First, since we can misidentify the world, we can also misidentify ourselves when prediction goes wrong; this gives psychiatry and neurology a chance to target mechanisms rather than only treating the symptoms of depression and schizophrenia. Second, "I am me" cannot be reduced to or uploaded into a software program running on some robot, no matter how smart or complex — we are creatures of flesh and blood, and conscious experience is shaped at every level by the biological mechanisms that keep us alive. Third, everyone has their own inner universe, and human consciousness is just a small region in a vast space of possible consciousness. So merely making computers smarter will not make them sentient.

terms.def: The brain actively generates experience while being constrained by sensory signals; normal perception is a controlled hallucination.
The brain's perception of visceral states such as heartbeat and blood pressure, whose goal is not identification but regulation and survival.
Perception is the brain's guess about the causes of the world, combining sensory signals with prior expectations.

quotes.text: Consciousness and intelligence are very different things. You don't have to be smart to suffer, but you probably do have to be alive.
We don't just passively perceive our worlds. We actively generate them.
In fact, we're all hallucinating all the time, including right now. It's just that when we agree about our hallucinations, that's what we call reality.
Perception of the internal state of the body isn't about figuring out what's there. It's about control and regulation.
Just making computers smarter is not going to make them sentient.
